1:
The safe return is read as a mercy measured against three worse outcomes. Henry sets them out in order: he fared better than he expected, having been in imminent peril and yet coming home in peace, so that whenever we return in safety we ought to acknowledge God's providence over our going out and coming in; better than he deserved, having been out of the way of his duty on an expedition he could not account for to God and his conscience, for God is not extreme to mark what we do amiss nor withdraw his protection the moment we forfeit it; and better than Ahab, who was brought home slain. Here were two kings in the field together, Henry says, one taken and the other left, one brought home in blood and the other in peace; and though Jehoshaphat had said to Ahab that he was as he was, God distinguished him. Ellicott notices the same contrast more briefly, the fate of Ahab being suggested by the wording, and would render in peace as in wholeness or soundness, that is unhurt. Clarke says only that he was safe notwithstanding a danger so imminent that none but the especial mercy of God could have saved him.

On the reproof the commentary dwells on the courage it took. Ellicott identifies Jehu as the son of the seer who had suffered for his reproof of Asa and had himself already witnessed against the king of Israel, and draws the point that the prophets never shrank from facing the highest representatives of earthly power. Gill notes the same from the family connection, that the father's imprisonment for reproving Asa did not deter his son. Henry adds that the father was an eminent prophet in the last reign, as appeared by Asa putting him in the stocks for his plain dealing, and the son was not afraid to reprove another king. Ellicott works the wording closely, rendering the charge as an infinitive, oughtest thou to help, with the ungodly as the emphatic word, and turning the second clause into a question of its own, and haters of the Lord lovest thou, the particle before haters being characteristic of the chronicler's style. Henry puts the charge as two questions: whether a godly man should help the ungodly by giving them a hand of fellowship and lending them a hand of assistance, and whether he should love those whom God beholds afar off.

What the threatened wrath was is the one question the chapter leaves open, and it is answered from two directions. Ellicott raises it as a problem of comparison: the same phrase is used of David, where the wrath was embodied in pestilence, so what form did it take here? He thinks the following chapters seem to supply the answer, beginning with the invasion of his land. Wesley answers it with three instances, that God chastised him partly by stirring up the Moabites and others to invade him, partly by permitting his eldest son to kill all his brothers, and principally by bringing an almost general destruction on his grandchildren, which he calls the fruit of the alliance with Ahab. Clarke declines the historical question and presses the application, asking whether the wrath of God is not upon all alliances his people form with the ungodly, whether social, matrimonial, commercial or political. On the mitigation all agree. Ellicott glosses it as meaning the wrath will not pursue him to destruction because there are good things found in him; Gill reads these as principles of grace and righteousness and holiness from which many good works sprang; Wesley calls them good marks from an honest heart, which God regards more than this particular error, so that he will chasten but not destroy. Ellicott adds that the removal of the groves had been Asa's work too, and would render the last clause directed rather than prepared.
4:
Whether Jehoshaphat made the circuit himself is a small point on which two voices divide. Clarke takes the boundary formula as evidence that he did: before the separation the extent of the land was given as from Dan to Beer-sheba, but since then Judah was bounded south by Beer-sheba and north by the mountains of Ephraim, so the phrase shows Jehoshaphat had gone through all his territories to examine everything himself. Ellicott denies the inference, holding that he went out not necessarily in person but by his accredited representatives, and treats the journey as a second visitation after the earlier commission for instructing the people in the law. On what the people were brought back from Ellicott is precise: not only from the Baals but from the illicit worship of Jehovah itself, and he quotes an account of how the two had assimilated, since the local worship of the God of Israel necessarily came into contact with the Canaanite service of Baal, and since the offerings of Jehovah, consecrating the good things of his bestowing, were in a land of corn and wine no longer the scanty products of pastoral life, so that the feasts grew more luxurious.

Wesley supplies the motive the others leave out, and it connects the reform to the rebuke. Many had probably revolted to idolatry on seeing their king so intimate with idolaters, and Jehoshaphat therefore thought himself doubly obliged to reduce them; from which Wesley draws the rule that if we truly repent of sin we shall do our utmost to repair the damage we have done to religion or to the souls of others. Gill reads the opening clause as a withdrawal, that Jehoshaphat went out no more to Samaria nor concerned himself with the affairs of Israel but attended to his own. Henry sets the judicial reform beside the earlier teaching mission: having sent preachers to instruct the people he now saw it requisite to send judges, to see the laws put in execution and be a terror to evil-doers; and he supposes there were judges before, but either they neglected their business or the people slighted them, so the institution had to be new-modelled with new men and a new charge.

On the charge the commentary converges and then sharpens. Henry divides it into two means and three motives. The means are great caution, since judges of all men have need of it because so much depends on the correctness of their judgment, and great piety, the fear of God being both a restraint and an engagement to activity, so that if destruction from God is a terror to them they will be a terror to none but evil-doers. The motives are all taken from God: that from him they had their commission, so their business is to glorify him and serve his kingdom among men; that his eye is upon them in the judgment, to take notice and call them to account; and that he is the great example of justice, there being no bribery nor respect of persons with him, magistrates being called gods and bound to resemble him. Ellicott renders the first motive as a denial, that it is not for man they will judge but for Jehovah as his vicegerents, and the second as a promise of presence, that Jehovah will be with them when they give sentence; and he notes that the Greek and Latin misunderstand the clause while the Syriac renders it that they should be strong and judge true judgment and the Lord would be with them for ever. He closes with two observations worth keeping: those who judge for Jehovah are bound to judge like Jehovah, and the king's own name means Jehovah judgeth. Clarke puts it in one line: judges should feel themselves in the place of God and judge as those who know they shall be judged for their judgments.
8:
Whether Jehoshaphat set up one court in Jerusalem or two is unsettled, and the voices fall four ways. Clarke is most definite: here was a twofold jurisdiction, ecclesiastical and civil, the high priest supreme judge in one and Zebadiah in the other, the Levites counsellors to both; and he presses it as a principle that the things of God and the things of the king should never be confounded in the administration of justice, the priest and the ruler ever having their distinct places of jurisdiction. Gill reads it as a single body, the great court of judicature consisting of princes, priests and Levites, of ecclesiastics and political persons together, since causes of both sorts were brought there. Henry takes the same view but with divided presidency, Amariah presiding in ecclesiastical causes and being last consulted in cases the judges themselves doubted of, and Zebadiah as prime minister presiding in all civil causes. Wesley declines to settle it, finding it not easy to determine whether these made up one court by which all causes were decided or two distinct courts, one of priests and Levites and one of the chief of the fathers. Ellicott describes the institution rather than its constitution, a high court of appeal in the capital such as Deuteronomy prescribes, with the high priest naturally president in spiritual cases and the tribal prince in civil ones, and the Levites as writers, inferior officials such as scribes and notaries acting under their direction.

The clause about returning to Jerusalem produces a textual disagreement, both sides arguing from the words. Clarke asks who it was that returned, and rejects the usual answer that Jehoshaphat and his court did so after the visitation, on the ground that if the text spoke of anyone returning to Jerusalem the preposition would be used and it is not; he reports with approval the conjecture that the word should read not and they returned but the inhabitants, giving the controversies of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Ellicott keeps the received reading and refers the return to the earlier royal commission, placing a full stop at controversies and noting that the Syriac and Arabic make the clause begin there. On the two kinds of cause Ellicott glosses the matter of the Lord as ecclesiastical and the controversies as litigation, and reads the triad of commandment and statutes and judgments as questions about the interpretation of the legal rules. Clarke divides them concretely, taking the questions of blood as cases of manslaughter or of consanguinity and inheritance, and those of law and commandment as whatever concerns the moral precepts and ceremonies or belongs to civil affairs.

Ellicott argues the high priest's identity from chronology: Amariah stands fifth from Zadok in the genealogy, and as Jehoshaphat was the fifth king from David the name probably denotes the same person in both places. Henry explains why homicide came to Jerusalem: after the revolt all the cities of refuge except Hebron belonged to the northern kingdom, so the courts of the temple or the horns of the altar were chiefly used as sanctuaries and the trial of homicides was reserved for the capital. On the duty of warning Ellicott has the judges teach the parties the true sense of the law in the particular case, so they do not incur guilt by false judgment, and observes that a miscarriage of justice would involve not the immediate agents only but the whole people in guilt and its penal consequences. Henry closes on the division of labour with evident pleasure: some best understand the matters of the Lord and others the king's matters, and neither can say to the other that it has no need of him, there being diversities of gifts but all from the same Spirit; blessed be God, he adds, both for magistrates and ministers, scribes and statesmen, men of books and men of business.
